newsitem.title: USA: Oil firms say Alaska could have gas line by 2005.
newsitem.headline: Oil firms say Alaska could have gas line by 2005.

text.p: A pipeline to export liquefied natural gas from Alaska's North Slope to Asia could be feasible in a decade if startup costs were reduced by at least a fifth, oil company officials said Tuesday.

Representatives of Exxon, British Petroleum and Atlantic Richfield, the major owners of the supergiant Prudhoe Bay oil field, gave that forecast at a hearing of a special committee of the state legislature.

Prudhoe Bay's 26 trillion cubic feet of natural gas offer a great commercial opportunity, but Alaskans must be patient while waiting for progress on the state's next big development project, the oil company representatives said.

"Our market analysis shows that there's virtually no (scenario) by which we can put Alaska gas into the market before 2005," said David Lawrence, gas commercialization and marketing manager for Arco Alaska Inc., owner of 32 percent of the Prudhoe gas cap.
The gas would be shipped to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the company officials said.
Building the project would cost an estimated $15 billion, said Jim Branch, Alaska production manager for Exxon, which owns 32 percent of the Prudhoe gas cap.
Company planners have identified options that could reduce that cost by $3 billion, Branch said.
"We are leaving all kinds of options open on evaluating the project," he said. "We want to look at all cost-reduction opportunities."

But the president of Yukon-Pacific Corp., the CSX Corp. subsidiary that holds permits for a gas pipeline that would parallel the existing 800-mile trans-Alaska oil pipeline, suggested those alternatives amounted to stall tactics.
"We have only one project here, and that's the bottom line," Yukon Pacific President Jeff Lowenfels told the lawmakers.
Yukon Pacific has been frustrated by lack of coooperation from the oil companies on the project, Lowenfels said.
He said he believed movement on the gas project was needed soon, or else other gas projects would take Alaska's place in the Asian market.
"Time is ticking. The market window could close on Alaska," he said.
British Petroleum unit BP Exploration (Alaska) Inc. owns 21 percent of the Prudhoe gas cap. The state of Alaska owns 12.5 percent of the gas cap.
With oil production on the North Slope declining since the 1988 peak of over 2 million barrels a day, state officials have looked increasingly at the potential for selling the area's natural gas.

Exxon, Arco and British Petroleum all have natural gas projects under way or planned elsewhere in the world, and some state lawmakers fear the companies have assigned the Alaska project a low priority.

"If we are displaced in the marketplace, then I think the displacement will be done by the major producers in Alaska," State Rep. Ramona Barnes, an Anchorage Republican who chairs the special committee, told the company representatives.
